summary:
Our project is an interactive space mission simulator designed to help students understand the engineering decisions involved in planning and executing space missions.

Players can choose between different exploration missions, design their spacecraft by selecting components and scientific instruments, and manage limited resources such as budget, mass, fuel and power. During the simulated flight, unexpected events require players to make decisions that influence mission performance and success.

The simulator combines mission planning, resource management and interactive decision-making in an engaging learning experience. It aims to make complex space engineering trade-offs easier to understand through experimentation and immediate feedback.
details:
Overview

MISSION CONTROL: Space Mission Simulator is a browser game where you play the mission director. You pick a destination (the Moon, an asteroid, or Mars), design a spacecraft within a budget, launch it, and find out in a debrief whether your design worked and why.

How it works

  1. Choose: Pick a mission. Each one has its own difficulty, budget, mass limit, sunlight level and science goals.
  2. Build: Select the engine, fuel tank, solar panels, antenna and science instruments. A live summary tracks money, mass, fuel needed versus carried, and power balance, with warnings before launch.
  3. Fly: Watch the animated countdown, launch, stage separation and cruise. Random events like faults and signal problems force quick decisions.
  4. Debrief: Get a score out of 100 and a rank from Cadet to Flight Director. The debrief covers mission success, science results, resource management and budget use, with plain-language advice on what went well and what to improve.

The core idea is trade-offs. Heavier craft need more fuel, efficient engines draw more power, and solar panels produce less power far from the Sun. Science objectives only count if you carried the right instrument, it survived, and its data was transmitted back to Earth.

Benefits and impact

The game teaches students and the public that space missions are about engineering decisions, not just launches. Players learn how mass, fuel, power, communications and cost affect each other, and that failure is a useful part of the process. It runs in any browser on desktop or mobile with no install or account, so it is easy to use in classrooms and at outreach events.

Tools and technologies

  • HTML5, CSS3 and vanilla JavaScript in one self-contained file
  • HTML Canvas API for all graphics (rocket, spacecraft, planets, stars, animation), drawn in code
  • Web Audio API for sound effects, synthesized in the browser with no audio files
  • Google Fonts (Barlow, Barlow Condensed)
  • NASA Solar System Exploration (https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/) as a reference for mission themes and science goals
  • Claude (Anthropic), a large language model, used to generate about half of the code. The team wrote the rest and reviewed, tested and modified all SI-generated code.

Team

A team of six. We handled the concept, game design, balancing, testing and writing, and wrote about half of the code ourselves.

Creativity

The game turns real engineering constraints into gameplay. Each destination changes the rules, so the design phase decides the outcome and no two missions feel the same. All visuals and sounds are generated by code, which keeps the game small and fast, and it uses no NASA logos or branding.

Factors we considered

  • Realistic trade-offs, simplified for gameplay (values are not real mission data)
  • Easy, Medium and Hard missions so beginners can start with the Moon
  • Scoring that penalizes both overspending and hoarding the budget
  • Clear, encouraging feedback, mobile support and no downloads
  • Transparent SI use: AI-assisted code is disclosed in the project’s metadata, code comments and on-page text
